name: ふる川 権堂店 (Furukawa Gondo)

claims.text: Hokkaido ramen noodles (wheat) are cooked tableside in the shared Jinhoru Nabe pot as the standard finishing course, creating direct gluten contact with the broth served to everyone at the table.
Yakiniku and jingisukan tare sauces in Japan standardly contain wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere in the restaurant's listings.
The restaurant serves only meat and offal; there is no plant-based cooking surface or equipment — full cross-contact with animal products throughout.

No allergen menu, allergy-handling policy, or staff training for dietary restrictions is mentioned in any available source. Phone enquiry (026-233-7357) before visiting is the only documented route for special requests.
No information on cross-contamination protocols has been published. The kitchen serves a traditional temple setting and no celiac-safe procedures have been confirmed.

Standard Japanese shojin ryori typically uses wheat-containing soy sauce (shoyu) for seasoning. Additionally, fu (wheat gluten cake) is a common shojin ingredient. Neither tamari nor gluten-free shoyu alternatives have been confirmed for this kitchen.
Shojin ryori is vegan by religious design — the Buddhist precepts governing the cuisine exclude all animal products from the kitchen, making cross-contact with meat or fish highly unlikely.

English-speaking staff are noted as available, which means allergy communication is possible, but no documented allergy protocol or allergen menu exists. Direct phone inquiry (026-232-2546) before visiting is strongly recommended for anyone with gluten sensitivity or celiac disease.
Cuisine is fully plant-based by Buddhist religious mandate — no meat, fish, eggs, or dairy, making it reliably vegan without need to interrogate individual dishes.
Day-visitor shojin lunch is available (minimum 5 people, reservation required at least 1 week ahead) at approximately ¥1,500 per person, making it accessible outside of overnight stays.

No information about cross-contamination protocols is available from any source reviewed. The kitchen handles miso, soy sauce (standard wheat-containing), sake lees, and fish sauce across all dishes, making a wheat-free environment highly unlikely.

Standard Japanese soy sauce is a core ingredient across the menu. Miso (which contains wheat in most Shinshu varieties) and fermented condiments are foundational to the entire concept. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned on any source.

Animal-derived fermented ingredients — fish sauce, fermented butter, yogurt, bonito-based sauces, sake-lees pork — are used throughout the kitchen. Vegan cross-contact in a shared kitchen is highly probable and no vegan protocols are disclosed.
No allergy-handling policy or allergen menu is mentioned on the official website, Tabelog, HotPepper, or any blog reviewed. The English website exists but contains no allergen disclosure section.
Full English website and international visitor orientation mean staff are likely more accustomed to dietary questions from non-Japanese guests than a typical izakaya. Calling ahead is feasible.
No information available on cross-contamination controls. The kitchen produces flour-based cakes and pastries daily; no allergen separation protocols have been reported in any source.
Soy sauce does not appear in the menu at all — this is a coffee and cake shop with no savory cooking.
All baked goods appear to contain dairy; no plant-based alternatives have been mentioned. Cross-contact between dairy-containing pastries and any theoretical vegan order cannot be ruled out.

No allergy-handling protocols or allergen menus have been reported by any source. The shop is a small two-person operation; direct inquiry by phone (050-3699-7897) or via Instagram (@hirano_coffee) before visiting is strongly recommended for anyone with serious dietary restrictions.
Plain black coffee (all varieties) is naturally gluten-free and vegan — the shop stocks 14–15 bean varieties and roasts almost daily, so coffee-only visits are low-risk.

name: 今むらそば 本店 (Imamura Soba Honten)

claims.text: No allergen or cross-contamination information is published. The kitchen prepares tempura (wheat batter) alongside soba, making shared-fryer cross-contact plausible.
Tsuyu (dipping sauce) at traditional Japanese soba restaurants is made with wheat-containing soy sauce (shoyu). No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned in any source.
The menu includes chicken (Shinshu Golden Shamo), duck (鴨せいろ), and tempura — animal products are central to the kitchen, making vegan cross-contact likely.

The Nagano City tourism board notes that the restaurant can 'consider religious dietary requirements upon consultation' and provides an English menu, suggesting some willingness to discuss dietary needs — though no English-speaking staff are confirmed.
The soba itself is 90% buckwheat (kuichi ratio), meaning it contains less wheat binder than standard soba — a marginal benefit for wheat-sensitivity (not celiac safety).

name: いろは堂 善光寺仲見世店 (Irohado Zenkoji Nakamise)

claims.text: Dough contains wheat flour as a primary ingredient — there is no gluten-free option and no separation from wheat. The fry-bake process uses the same soybean oil for all varieties. Celiac diners must avoid.

No soy sauce appears in published ingredient lists. Seasoning is Shinshu miso (soy-based) and salt. Miso inherently contains soy but the declared allergens are wheat, buckwheat, and soy — soy sauce as a separate wheat-bearing additive is not listed.

All standard varieties appear plant-based; no animal products identified in ingredient lists. A shared production line note mentions sesame and apple but no mention of dairy or egg lines. Cross-contact with animal products is not documented as a risk, but the facility is not certified vegan.

No documented allergy-handling protocol for the Nakamise stall. Counter service is fast-paced temple-street takeout; detailed allergen queries are best directed to Irohado's main customer service line (026-217-6636) before visiting.

Published ingredient lists for standard varieties — nozawana, green onion miso, vegetable mix, kiriboshi daikon, mushroom, pumpkin, bean paste — show no dashi, bonito, eggs, or dairy; all fillings are vegetable and miso-based.
Miso seasoning is a customized Shinshu miso sourced from a local established miso maker; no fish-based dashi listed as an ingredient in any variety.

name: 大福とウイスキーの店 いづみや民藏 (Izumiya Tamizo — Daifuku and Whiskey Bar)

claims.text: No information available on kitchen cross-contamination practices; the bar operates out of a small renovated kitchen space with no GF protocols documented.
Food items such as oden typically rely on soy sauce (which contains wheat) in the broth; no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Sausage and other meat-based snacks are served in the same small bar space; vegan cross-contact risk from shared preparation surfaces is unknown.

No allergy-handling procedures or staff training information is documented for this venue; the master operates largely alone at a 13-seat bar, so direct verbal communication with him is the only practical route.
Neat whiskey and spirits are naturally gluten-free; a primarily drinks-focused visit carries minimal dietary risk for GF drinkers who skip the food accompaniments.

name: 十割そば 大善 (Juuwari Soba Daizen)

claims.text: Tempura and fried side dishes (wheat batter) are prepared in the same kitchen as the GF soba. No dedicated fryer or separate preparation area is documented. Celiac diners should stick to plain soba and wheat-free tsuyu and skip all fried items.
Tsuyu uses wheat-free tamari soy sauce (田舎たまり醤油 / 本醸造たまり醤油) aged 3 months — this is explicitly wheat-free and is the restaurant's stated GF credential.
Dashi is fish/seafood-based (魚介系). No vegan broth alternative is offered. All soba dishes are served with this dashi-based tsuyu.

No formal allergy protocol documented. The wheat-free soy sauce is a built-in kitchen choice, not a made-to-order accommodation. Staff speak limited English; communicating specific celiac needs will require Japanese or a written card.
Soba noodles are 100% buckwheat (no wheat binder) and the tsuyu uses wheat-free tamari soy sauce — both the noodle and broth are intrinsically wheat-free by design, not as a special accommodation.
The wheat-free tamari tsuyu is house-made and aged 3 months using additive-free ingredients, giving both dietary safety and depth of flavour.
